summary: healing-agent is a Python decorator library that wraps functions with LLM-powered exception recovery. When a decorated function raises, it captures the full runtime context (stack trace, local/global variables, function source via AST), redacts secrets, sends it to an LLM (Azure/OpenAI/Anthropic/Ollama/LiteLLM), receives fixed code back, validates the fix via `compile()`, backs up the original source file, replaces the function in the AST on-disk, hot-reloads the module, and retries execution — all transparently. The actual code confirms the decorator lifetime: try-block wraps execution, on exception it lazy-imports exactly 6 modules, loads a config from `~/.healing_agent/`, captures rich context (source AST, call arguments, local/global variable previews), runs name-based secret redaction over the context dict, sends a structured prompt to a configurable AI broker, uses AST-level `astor`-based code replacement for the function body, and `importlib.reload`-style module re-execution to pick up the fix. Verdict is that this is a clever experiment with 19 commits, 2 distinct maintainers, and v0.2.6 — it is useful for quick recovery of simple, deterministic functions but brittle for stateful or side-effecting code and not production-hardened.

findings.description: Verified from actual source: (1) Decorator-based function wrapping that only imports heavy deps on exception (lazy import of inspect, sys, importlib); (2) AST-based function source capture via `ast.FunctionDef` traversal; (3) Structured exception context capture including frame locals/globals, traceback frames, function signature, call arguments; (4) Name-based secret redaction via regex matching against keys/variable names before writing to disk or sending to AI; (5) Configurable AI provider routing — Azure OpenAI, direct OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, and LiteLLM — with a broker pattern; (6) Prompt construction with function source code, error trace, arguments, and AI-generated hints; (7) `compile()`-based syntax validation of generated fixes; (8) AST-based (`astor`) function replacement in source files, stripping old function node and inserting the LLM output; (9) Hot module hot-reload via `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` + `exec_module` + `getattr`; (10) Optional `ImportError`/`ModuleNotFoundError` auto-install via pip; (11) Backup creation and exception context JSON saving to disk; (12) AI hint generation as a separate LLM call before the repair call.

apiSurface: The one and only API is `@healing_agent` — a dual-use decorator that can be applied as `@healing_agent` or `@healing_agent(AUTO_FIX=False, DEBUG=True)`. After decoration, a function runs normally unless an exception occurs. On exception it prints to stdout (not a logger), attempts an LLM fix, optionally rewrites the source file, optionally reloads the module, and either returns the fixed result or None. Optional AUTO_SYSCHANGE parameter controls whether missing-module auto-install triggers before entering the fix flow.
integrationPoints: This library integrates at the Python code level, not at the pipeline level. For Veridian: the context-capture subsystem (exception_handler.py) could inform Playwright error telemetry — capturing the exact line, local variables, and page state on failure. The redactor pattern (regex-based name matching) is reusable for scrubbing API keys before logging. The AI broker pattern (provider-routing factory) is a lightweight multi-LLM dispatcher that matches the poly-LLM design of the Veridian pipeline. The most direct use would be a healing guard around flaky browser interactions: if a Playwright operation raises after N retries, send the page snapshot + selector + error to an LLM for diagnosis.
strengthsForVeridian: (1) The lazy-import-on-error pattern (only imports heavyweight modules when exception occurs) keeps overhead zero during normal operation — useful for high-throughput scraping where most calls succeed; (2) The AI broker pattern provides a clean abstraction for provider routing that could fit Veridian's need for provider-optional configuration; (3) The redactor module is well-documented and genuinely thoughtful about preventing credential leaks; (4) The compile()-based validation of LLM output before writing to disk is a necessary guard against bad LLM output; (5) The AST-based source capture gets the actual source code, not `inspect.getsource()` approximations, which could matter for Playwright script generation where the source text is what gets sent to the LLM; (6) Backup-before-modify is enabled by default.
weaknessesForVeridian: (1) The tool rewrites source files — for a scraping pipeline this is inappropriate: Veridian needs a reliable script that runs deterministically; hot-fixing in production is dangerous; (2) No logging framework — all output uses `print()` to stdout with decorative separators, which is noisy and non-capturable in a pipeline; (3) `MAX_ATTEMPTS=3` is defined in config but unused — there is exactly one fix attempt per exception, which means it either works or you get nothing; (4) The LLM fix-then-reload pattern means stateful scrapers lose state — after a module reload, any global caches, TLS sessions, or open file handles are toasted; (5) Heavy dependency on LLM calls per exception (two calls: hint generation + code fix) — this is expensive for a pipeline that expects N repeated site scrapes; (6) The library is fundamentally designed for interactive Python development workflows, not headless pipeline use; (7) Only a single maintainer with infrequent commits; (8) The generated JSON context files grow large quickly and there is no rotation or cleanup mechanism.
limitations: Seeded from prior analysis; maturity signals may be approximate
